Advanced Uses

Part 2: Parallel Lists
Creating multiple separate, yet
related lists.

Parallel Lists
Parallel lists are separate lists
names = ["Alex", "Sam", "Jordan"]
where values at the same index
scores = [82, 91, 76]
are related to one another.
They are useful when you want
to keep different types of

collections. print(scores[1])
The lists must stay in the same
order so that matching indices OUTPUT

Creating Related Lists
Two (or more) related lists
names = ["Alex", "Sam", "Jordan"]
can be created by storing
grades = [82, 91, 76]
matching data at the same
index in each list.
For example, one list can
print(f"{names[0]}: {grades[0]}")
store student names while
another stores their grades.
Index 0 in both lists refers to
OUTPUT
the same student, index 1 Alex: 82
refers to the next student,
and so on.

enumerate()
Traversing with
The enumerate() function names = ["Alex", "Sam", "Jordan"]
provides both the index
grades = [82, 91, 76]
and the value from a list
during traversal.
for i, name in enumerate(names):
The index can then be
print(f"{name}: {grades[i]}")
used to access the related
value in another list.

zip()
Traversing with
The zip() function combines names = ["Alex", "Sam", "Jordan"]
matching values from multiple
grades = [82, 91, 76]
lists during traversal.
This allows related values to be
for name, grade in zip(names, grades):
accessed directly without
print(f"{name}: {grade}")
manually working with indices.
zip() is often the simplest
option when you only need the
matching values. OUTPUT
